utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are following these proceedings. At the outset of today's hearing, I would like to give some guidance about the timings of the 98 bis proceedings. We will soon be breaking for -- today, in fact, for four weeks, and when we return, the Prosecution case can be expected to continue for a relatively short amount of time. However, it would be premature at this stage to set a dead-line by which the Prosecution case is to be completed. The Chamber, nevertheless, considers that it will assist everyone if it gives an indication of the time-lines that it is intending to follow in the procedure pursuant to Rule 98 bis. In drawing up these time-lines, the Trial Chamber has been particularly mindful of its obligation under Article 20(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal to ensure that the trial is fair and expeditious. The time-lines that the Trial Chamber intends to implement are as follows: If the accused wishes to make oral submissions pursuant to Rule 98 bis, he should do so one week after the end of the Prosecution case. The accused's oral submissions should last no more than three hours. On the court day after the accused makes his submissions, the Prosecution may make oral submissions in response. The Prosecution's oral submissions should also last no more than three hours. On the court day after the response of the Prosecution, the Defence should have an opportunity to reply, and the reply should be limited to one hour. On a day in the week after the end of the submissions of the parties pursuant to Rule 98 bis, the Trial Chamber will issue its oral decision. Just to ensure that there is no doubt, I should say that by "a court day," I mean a day on which the court sits. Therefore, weekends and Tribunal holidays are excluded. The Trial Chamber believes that the time-lines just given are the most appropriate, but it does not rule out the possibility of minor adjustments in light of future developments. I don't see anybody on his feet. No comments by the parties. In that case, the witness should be brought in. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Just some translations I could -- should read into the record, as per our practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can postpone that for a little bit. The Chamber -- the staff of the Chamber is checking some problems with that, and we could do that perhaps after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. Welcome back again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps there's no need for it, but I have to remind you again that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies also for today. Mr. Tolimir, you may continue your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. May there be peace in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings. And I would like to wish a pleasant stay to Mr. Butler here in this courtroom with all of us participants in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Now, could we see P2369 in e-court, please. That's a document of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Republic, the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the BH Army, and it was drafted on the 9th of November, 1995. And it is entitled "The Basic Guide-Lines for the Mission," and it was submitted to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear to whom it was submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Two matters. Mr. Tolimir, the number of this document in the transcript can't be the right one, and please repeat the end of your introduction: "It is submitted to the ..." And then it stops. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is P2369. That is the exhibit that we wanted to pull up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, you said: "And it is submitted to the ..." And then the transcript stops. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said the basic concept for the mission, and it is sent to the Command of the Operative Group in Srebrenica. And that's where I stopped - thank you - if that's what was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we gave you, at your request, this document so that you can study it. Now, can you tell us whether you've been able to read through it, and could you tell the Trial Chamber what this is about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and good morning. I have reviewed this document. It is a detailed plan and proposal which discusses a, rather, series of complex and synchronised military attacks by forces of Operation Group 8, the ABiH 2 Corps, and a number of other formations that they were planning to undertake at some future point in Eastern Bosnia. It involved -- as military operations goes, this one had a lot of moving parts, so it did require a good deal of co-ordination between the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of the BH, ABiH 2 Corps, and OG-8 in order to have a chance of succeeding under the circumstances. So this particular document reflects, to a large degree, part of the detailed planning that those three organisations were undertaking in order to realise this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could you tell us now, please, whether we can see from this plan that the Main Staff -- or, rather, the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in direct contact with the Srebrenica Operation Group and that it co-ordinated and planned its activities around Srebrenica together with that operations group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to this document - and just to make one minor correction: the document is dated 9 November 1994, the transcript said "1995" - it does reflect that at least in this particular case the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of the BiH were communicating not only to 2 Corps, but also directly to Operations Group 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether Operations Group 8 is, in fact, the 28th Division from Srebrenica? This is necessary from the transcript because this is the first time that we've used this term.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. And at some point in early 1995 the organisation known as Operations or Operative Group 8 is redesignated as the 28th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, is this the basic plan for active combat operations of the 28th Division from the demilitarised zone in Srebrenica, the 2nd Corps from Tuzla, and other forces of the 2nd force, including forces from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a document that is still a conceptual plan. It is not actually, with respect to the initiation of those combat operations, an implementation order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph item 1 of this document, where it says: "The plan is -- the concept is: Liberate through active combat part of the temporarily seized territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the municipalities of Bratunac, Vlasenica, Sekovici, Zvornik, Kalesija, and link them up with the free territories of Zepa and Srebrenica," or, rather, "link the free territories of Zepa and Srebrenica with the free territories of Zvornik, Kalesija, and Sekovici in order to create a permanent free corridor for the supply of the population and logistic support to the units of the BH Army and the basis for further liberation of North-Eastern Bosnia as a whole." So is this the basic concept for future combat actions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please take a look at the following paragraph, below the one that I've just quoted. It says: "The borders of the corridor," "Corridor Borders." Now we see it in the English version as well. And it says: "The village of Podzeplje (the free territory of Zepa), the village of Barice, Sokolica, from Gorijela [phoen] (trig point 431), the village Brezova Glava, Koprivno, Rogac, Mratinjsko Brdo, Previla, Nova Kasaba, Pobujica [phoen]" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And so on and so forth. Are all these places of the corridor in the territory that you studied in the Srebrenica and Zepa sectors, and are the axes -- or, rather, the directions that lead to the 2nd Corps, is this the indication of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not having the ability to plot these particular locations on a map, it's kind of abstract. But I do recognise, obviously, a number of villages as being in the territory of the Republika Srpska at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's take a look at the right border of the future corridor, or intended corridor. It says: "Brestovik (trig point 1291)," and then another bracket" (Zepa territory), Stublic stream, Krcevine (trig point 806), Pale village, Bijelo Polje village, Bucje, Slapovic, Sarici village, further following the border of the free territory of Srebrenica up to Borici village, Zagoni village, Magasici village, Vladusici village, Tusto Brdo (trig point 664), Ocenovici village, Panjevici village (trig point 665) Drenjak (trig point 771), Graina (trig point 693), Kuslat village, Kostjerovo village, Drinjaca village, the left bank of the Drina up to the fortress ..." Now, having the starting point in Zepa, which is Brestovik, trig point 1291, and knowing the left border of the Drina all the way to the forest, can you now orientate yourself to figure out what the border of the corridor is? And he goes on to then mention: "... Kula, the town of Zvornik, Marcici village, Markovaca (trig point 372), Kolovnik village, Percini, Jardan village, Sapna River upstream to Vrela Strana village (these features are to be connected by a line)." Do you now have a picture of where the corridor is, in view of the fact that it ends at Sapna River and begins at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one clarification. I believe the document says "Kula Grad," and I don't know if the translation didn't get that, but I just -- Kula Grad and Kula are two very distinct and different places that are important in this case, so I just want to make sure that that is clear. As I see this, it says "Kula Grad Zvornik," and I think the general just said "Kula," but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, would you agree that we see in the document "Kula Grad Zvornik"? In line 22 of page 7 you are recorded as having said "Kula."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. It is Kula Grad in Zvornik, and that is why I read out that name, so that the witness could recognise it; the location, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, do you we see now that this area stretches all the way from Zepa to Sapna River, which is in the territory of the BH Federation, and is it, as noted here, the right border that should be drawn up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The document reflects that this is the right-hand border of the proposed corridor or main axis of the attack. And as, you know, both I note and, I presume at this juncture, the Court notes, many of these villages that are mentioned are in the Bratunac and Zvornik municipalities. So this territory is in what is at the time and still is part of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we've seen the left and the right border of the corridor that is supposed to run from Srebrenica and Zepa towards the area of the Tuzla Corps, can we now -- let's now take a look at item 2, where it says the manner of executing of this task: "Liberate the temporarily seized sector of the corridor, inserting large forces into the depth of the corridor sector, and engaging in offensive operations from the free territories of OG-4, OG-6 of the 2nd Corps, and OG-8 Srebrenica." Liberate the temporarily seized corridor along the lines as given in item 1: "Engage the already-prepared logistics support immediately through the 2nd Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, these are -- you are reading many technical and geographical terms. This is quite difficult for the interpreters to get everything, and especially for the court reporter. If you want to have it on the record, you should slow down while reading, especially if you are dealing with so many technical and geographical terms. Now your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do my best to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we discussed many different technical terms here, so now I would like to ask you what OG-4 and OG-6 of the 2nd Corps are and what the OG-8 of Srebrenica is that are supposed to liberate the indicated territory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar exactly which particular units OG-4 and OG-6 are. I assume that just like OG-8 becomes the 28th Division of the ABiH 2nd Corps, that OG-4 and OG-6 ultimately become the 24th and 26th Division of the 2nd Corps. Again, we've discussed Operations Group 8, which later becomes the 28th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for clarifying this. Now, please take a look at item 3. It says "Engagement of forces," and then 3.1, "OG-8 Srebrenica forces." And then it mentions the 284th Eastern Bosnia Light Infantry Brigade which will be used in order to insert itself into the depth of the corridor, and combat groups of battalion strength. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what these operations group of Srebrenica forces are, and what is the area of -- what was the role and place of the 284th Eastern Bosnia Light Infantry Brigade in the 28th Division of the Srebrenica area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, it was envisioned that the 284th Light Infantry Brigade would be the primary offensive force for OG-8 in conducting this activity. As one reads down through the various subcomponents of paragraph 3.1 - this goes to A, B, C, and on the subsequent pages - it lists out in specific detail where various subcomponents of the brigade are expected to attack, what their objectives would be, and what axis they will travel to get to those particular objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. To avoid looking at each group and subgroup, can you just -- you've mentioned them. We can just mention that it says, under 8, "Combat group 1," as part of the 284th Eastern Bosnia Light Infantry Brigade, and then it goes on to say the "first subgroup," "second subgroup," "third subgroup." Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what these subgroups of the first combat group are? And they are discussed in paragraph 3.1(A).

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document, what it talks about in combat groups, it identifies a combat group as an element that is the equivalent of battalion strength. So when one starts talking about subgroups, you are talking about elements below battalion. So, you know, in your first subgrouping you would be talking about company organisations. If you were to further divide that, you would be talking platoon-level organisations. It says -- I should say "platoon." It says "balloon" on the transcript. There you go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for the correction. Please, let us look under "A, Combat Group 1," where it says: "Elements of the 284th East Bosnia Light Brigade, the former 6th Detachment, Kamenica, upon the decision of the commander, go to Snagovo and connect these points by a line in an irregular circle. Divide this group into four subgroups. Send them along the axis, and take control of the features as follows:" And then he mentions what facilities will be taken by what groups. Please tell us, does this mean that the 284th Brigade is hereby divided into several combat groups and that only the first combat group is composed of its 4th Detachment? And is the 4th Detachment supposed to advance to Snagovo and Djafin Kamen? Those lines are known to the Trial Chamber from some previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, what I would note is that it's not the only combat group. If one looks through this order, there are a total of four combat groups that are identified and tasks provided to them. But in this particular context, I mean, these are the orders for the first combat group, and it is envisioned under this plan that this particular combat group at some point would depart from the former enclave, would make their way to these various locations, and would occupy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, since we have just looked at the first combat group, could you please look at B and tell us whether the second combat group and the third combat group and the fourth combat group are also from the 284th Brigade, and does this mean that the entire brigade was supposed to infiltrate and advance to the borders of the corridor which is specified in the basic concept or the basic plan?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It does appear from this particular document that most of the combat forces are coming from the 284th Brigade, and one of the key items is, and as noted by General Tolimir, was that it's not envisioned that this is going to be an assault. What this envisions is a plan to, unit by unit, infiltrate these particular groups and subgroups out of the enclave and that they were going to occupy these various terrain features and locations, but they were going to seek to do so in a manner that would not alert the VRS that they were undertaking this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. After the infiltration of the brigade within the corridor and within the boundaries that we mention, in paragraph 3.2 on page 8 it says: "The other forces of the OG Srebrenica ..." We can see it now on the screen. It says here: "The strength and units participating will be decided by the OG-8 commander. Organise and carry out the following tasks:" And now we can see six tasks. For example, let us read out the second task and even the first task: "Organise stronger forces according to your decision, from the free area of the villages of Bljeceva village ... organise an attack along the Bljeceva village, Blazijevici village (trig point 532), Radukici village, Magasici village axis, and destroy the Chetniks in the sector of the Magasici village and along the axis of the attack. Organise co-ordination with the inserted forces." My question is this: After the insertion of the 284th Light Brigade and after they took the facilities that we mentioned, was it envisioned that the OG-8 Srebrenica carried out attacks and link up with the inserted forces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In this context, once the infiltrated forces were in position, it was envisioned that the remaining units of OG-8 would then attack the VRS positions outside of the enclave, working their way to link up with these units. And I would also note that, presumably as part of this exact same operation and at the same time, you would have the forces of OG-4 and OG-6 conducting offensive operations. Again, a rather complex operation with an enormous amount of moving parts. But I suspect that if the ABiH were able to pull this off, it would have made for a very interesting few days for the Drina Corps trying to figure out just what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Since you have just mentioned OGs 4 and 6 and since you said that they were also supposed to carry out attacks, can you tell us whether those OGs were in the territory under the control of the BH Army and whether they were supposed to carry out attacks from the front-line and launch an attack against the Serb forces that were defending themselves from the BiH Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That, in fact, would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're not going to read out all the six tasks. We're just going to read the second task because of the names of the places that the Trial Chamber is already familiar with and because of the activities that ensued. Paragraph 2 reads: "Organise stronger forces (according to your decision) from the free area of the villages of the Jaglici, Susnjari, and Kojsina (trig point 516) to carry out an attack along the Jaglici village-Lupoglav (trig point 676 [as interpreted])- Ravna Gora-Djermani village general axis, and proceed with an attack along the following three axes:" And I will stop quoting from the document at this point. I will just say that under bullet point 2 on one of those axes there is also a reference to Kravica village. My question is this: Was the 28th Division starting to break through from this position, from Jaglici village and Susnjari village, and was it advancing in the direction of Lupoglav while it was trying to break through from the enclave? Did you encounter this in your documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, these are well-defined routes by which supplies did go in and out of the enclave, and, logically, they were the paths that the 28th Division, or the column, as it were, in July 1995 took as it was leaving the Srebrenica -- the then fallen enclave and attempting to make their way into ABiH territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for your explanation. Please, under 3.2, there are 10 tasks covering 10 axes and 10 parts of the 28th Division. I don't have enough time to read all that. Let's just look at 3.3, referring to the Zepa forces, unless you have something else to add about Srebrenica. I will gladly give you the floor to do that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, the -- the tasks here in this document are relatively straightforward with respect to 1 through 10, so I don't have anything to add at this juncture, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And now we will just outline some of the things from bullet point 3.3, entitled "Zepa forces." We can now see it in English, 3.3, "Zepa forces," where it says in the first sentence: "The strength and the unit to participate are decided by the commander of the 1st Zepa Brigade. Organise and carry out the following tasks:" Does it show from this that Zepa was also involved in the operation as part of the forces of the 28th Division, or the OG, as they call it in here? OG-8 Srebrenica, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This document does lay out a role for the Zepa Brigade to participate and co-ordinate their combat operations with OG-8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we are going to read from paragraph 2 of Chapter 3.3. Can it be shown, because I would like to read a very typical and recognisable paragraph 2, where it says, and I read: "Engage a certain strength (as decided by the 1st Zepa Brigade commander) from the free area, from the Radava sector, along the Radava-Oglavci-Jazavicija Rupa-Karaula-Podravno village-Rupovo Brdo village axis, attack the Chetniks, disperse them on the axis of attack (if there are any), and co-ordinate with OG-8 Srebrenica forces in order to destroy the Chetniks in the sector of Rupovo Brdo village. Agree this co-ordinated action personally." My question is this: Do you perhaps know that forces from Srebrenica and Zepa on the 26th of June, before those forces were finally engaged, forayed along this axis and into the sectors which are outlined in here? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, I believe that one of the documents that I talked about during questioning by the Prosecutor was a document from the Zepa Brigade which may very well have, in fact, discussed this particular operation and the results of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask the e-court to show D62. Let's see if we are talking about the same document. And let us see if the activities evolved in keeping with the plan of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would kindly ask the e-court to display D62. Thank you. I would like to thank the e-court. We can see the document issued by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It has "Strictly Confidential," there's a number. The document was issued in Zepa on the 28th of June, 1995. The operative time was 1315 hours. This was sent to the 2nd Corps Command, to the 28th Division Command in Srebrenica, as you can see. And now could we please look at the signature -- or, rather, whose name is indicated on the document. Can we show that for the benefit of the witness. Thank you. You can see that here at the end it says "Commander, Colonel Avdo Palic." Can we go back to the first page. Thank you. I would like to read just one part of the combat report which was sent to the 2nd Corps Command and the 28th Division Command in Srebrenica. I'm quoting from the first paragraph, where it says: "Based on the order of the deputy commander of the 28th Division, Srebrenica, Major Ramiz Becirovic, Strictly Confidential number," so and so, "dated 20 June, 1995, on measures to be taken for the execution of sabotage actions aimed at inflicting losses upon the aggressor in terms of troops and equipment, and, in general, at turning Chetnik forces away from Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question: Did the commander of the Zepa Brigade write that he carried out the insertion of his groups in keeping with the orders received from the 28th Division in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The brigade command at Zepa did author this combat report to, one, reflect what he did once he received the orders, as well as discuss issues relating to their results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And now can we look at the second paragraph: "Upon receipt of the orders given me by brigade commanders Major Zulfo Tursunovic and Major Ibrahim Mandzic, and by the assistant for intelligence in the division, Captain Ekrem Salihovic, I reviewed the overall situation with respect to this kind of combat action, and based on earlier instructions issued to the Chief of Staff, Major Ramo Cardakovic, by the Chief of General Staff, Brigadier General Enver Hadzihasanovic, I decided, together with Tursunovic and Mandzic, to proceed as follows:" My question, based on the second paragraph, is this: Do you know who Zulfo Tursunovic and Ibrahim Mandzic are? Does the name of Ekrem Salihovic ring a bell? What I'm asking you is whether you have ever come across their names in any of the documents you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names sound familiar. And where I would have come across these names, for the most part, would have been either in 28th Infantry Division documents that I reviewed or in VRS documents where they are identifying individuals whom are in positions of authority within the 28th Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it transpire from the second paragraph of the combat report sent by Avdo Palic that the members of the 28th Division from Srebrenica, Zulfo Tursunovic, Ibrahim Mandzic, and Ekrem Salihovic, acted in concert with Ibrahim Mandzic; in other words, did they follow Mandzic's orders? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There should, I take it, be a mistake. Ibrahim Mandzic can't follow orders of Ibrahim Mandzic. Perhaps you misspoke or it is an interpretation issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Major Zulfo Tursunovic -- Mr. Butler, Major Zulfo Tursunovic, Ibrahim Mandzic, and Captain Ekrem Salihovic acted in concert with Avdo Palic, and did they work out the plan of attack which is mentioned in here in paragraph 3? It says that they had set up nine different groups and sent them out to carry out different tasks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I agree with your assertion, in the second paragraph, that Palic is working in concert with the other brigade commanders. I take the phrase "upon receipt of the orders given to me by brigade commanders" not to mean that Palic is somehow subordinate to them, but I take it more on a linguistic -- he has got a copy of the orders that they have given their particular units, and in reviewing them with the chief of intelligence, he is now putting together his own plan so they can, in fact, come up with a co-ordinated operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. But were you able to observe that in this first paragraph of the document it says: "Based on the order of the deputy commander of the 28th Division ..." So does that mean that the 28th Division is a superior command to the Zepa Brigade, where they sent these officers in order for the tasks to be carried out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Clearly, in this context, and again to be clear, I'm not saying that Major Becirovic does not exercise control or command over the Brigade Commander Palic, but I just want to be clear that, you know, certainly he takes his orders from the 28th Infantry Division. But in the context of the second paragraph, it reads that he was provided the orders of the brigade commanders of the other two units in order for him to co-ordinate his activities with those units and ensure that they were operating in co-operation with each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps because of the differences between the Serbian and English language there has been a misunderstanding, and I would appreciate it if the interpreters did not just read the text out from the screen, but, rather, to interpret what I say. In other words, "after I received the order which was handed in to me," in other words, this means that it was given by one person to another person, from hand to hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, thank you for your previous answer. Now, I don't want to read out the rest, but you probably noticed that in the third paragraph of this document that begins with the word: "Form a number of sabotage groups ..." and then it lists out nine groups below, and under number 1, as you can see, it says "Han Kram," among other things in brackets, and then so on and so forth. Now, the bracketed place names were actually features. Can we see that in paragraph 6, it says that "Crna Rijeka" group, and then "(monument)," does this show that these sabotage operations were carried out against certain features of the VRS Army outside of the territory of demilitarised zone of Zepa and Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were referring to paragraph 6, but I see this term in the line starting with the words "Group 5." Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And to answer the general's question: I recognise that a number of these particular features, and again just off the top of my head, fall outside the established boundaries of the enclaves. So in this context, these sabotage groups are leaving the enclaves to conduct raids that would be deep within the territory of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we should stay with the previous page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Butler just answered my question, and now I would need the next page in the English version for my next question, and we can stay on the same page in the Serbian language because the text is right before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at paragraph 2 in the English version, which is paragraph 3 below the numbers in the Serbian. And I'm just reading the first sentence, and I quote: "All DIV groups had the task of attacking at the same time of day, at two-hour intervals, with a view to stretching Chetnik forces ..." This report clearly says that all these groups, 1 through 9, actually engaged and acted at the same time in this two-hour interval. Is that what it says there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, what the paragraph -- the paragraph notes that that was the plan, that they were all going to carry out the actual combat part of these missions within the same time. However, I think if you go to the last two or three sentences of that paragraph, it does indicate that a number of the combat groups, for different reasons, were not able to undertake the combat actions and made a -- made a decision to withdraw. So, in fact, it appears from this document that only about half of the units actually managed to implement the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. However, can you see, in the last paragraph in Serbian, which is the third paragraph in English, where it says: "About 40 Chetniks were killed and dozens were wounded. A significant quantity of infantry weapons were seized ..."? And then it lists what weapons. It says 5.000 rounds and other military equipment. One aggressor soldier in the sector of Vrani Kamen was captured, likely wounded in the chest. His name is Velimir Mrdjan. My question is this: Can we see that the effect of these sabotage groups was tremendous and that these were far -- that these were higher losses than Zepa had throughout the rest of the war, according to their reports? Are these enormous losses in two hours of fighting, losses that were inflicted by this -- by a number of these sabotage reconnaissance groups?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this report is accurate with respect to the number of killed and wounded, it would be a significant combat loss. Forty killed and dozens wounded would represent a significant adverse impact to the unit that fell into this particular ambush or loss. Where -- when I recognised this and saw this, it's -- for me, at this juncture in time, it's hard to confirm whether these were, in fact, the actual losses incurred, because what I don't have possession of is the corresponding VRS documents which would reflect, presumably, what their actual casualties were during that operation. I can't -- I can't tell from this particular passage alone even what military unit of the VRS would have been garrisoned there, so I just don't have an ability at this point to confirm that the losses that are being reported by the ABiH in this document are, in fact, accurate, and what the VRS is reporting in their combat reports. I presume it can be a fact that is relatively easy to verify if the Office of the Prosecutor has the corresponding combat reports for whatever unit was attacked. But, you know, setting that issue aside, if the report is accurate, it would represent a significant combat loss to whatever unit was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now, are you aware that during the demilitarisation of Zepa this same soldier, whose name is mentioned here as having been captured, in other words, Velimir Mrdjan, was exchanged in 1997 and that he was in a position to begin with the evacuation, and then the VRS demanded that all the captured prisoners be released, and that this column was headed by this same soldier, Velimir Mrdjan? Would that confirm or corroborate the validity of this report if you were shown that other document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first answer that I have is, no, I'm not aware of that particular situation. It certainly would confirm the validity of the fact that this particular individual was captured. But, again, as you are aware, General, reports of damage and casualties that military units inflicted on other military units historically tend to be exaggerated in the heat of battle. So I'm not doubting that the incident occurred. What I'm saying is that I think that the number of dead and wounded that are being initially reported by Zepa seems higher than one might normally expect in a combat operation like this, and that there is a chance that the Zepa Infantry Brigade, either deliberately or inadvertently, exaggerated the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I understand what you're saying. But would you tell me, please, did the Zepa Brigade, which was in a demilitarised zone, was it entitled, did it have the right, to carry out combat operations against civilians? And I can tell you that we've heard witnesses here who testified to the liberation of this soldier, Velimir Mrdjan, and I also have to tell you that I have no reason to conceal anything here or exaggerate, and that the losses were even higher than shown here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And to be clear, I'm certainly -- I hope it's not an issue of translation. I'm not saying that you are potentially exaggerating this. The point that I am saying is that in combat environments there -- it is normal that the initial reports, particularly relating to casualties that one unit inflicts on another unit, tend to be inaccurate. I would recall back to the Kravica 1993, where, you know, the initial reports of casualties suffered by the Serbs, as the situation became clearer, those numbers went down to some degree. So it's simply a situation of the initial reports are often inaccurate, and as time goes by, more accurate reporting becomes available. I'm not implying that you would be exaggerating the situation. The second question is -- as I've testified with respect to questions asked by the Prosecutor, it is never legitimate to make civilians the object of a military attack, at least under the provisions of International Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. But does it make sense to you, if Han Pijesak was the place where the Main Staff was, and Crna Rijeka, and if this was deep in the territory, and if the Zepa area was demilitarised, was it logical that greater losses could be inflicted to civilians and to the army which does not expect such raids deep on their own territory? Would that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would certainly make sense that raids conducted by surprise against military forces that are not or have no advance notice of these raids would generate a number of casualties. Surprise, as you're aware, is something that is highly desired when planning military operations because it gives you a significant advantage on the battle-field. So in the sense of, you know, a raid conducted deep in enemy territory against troops who might not be alerted to such a possibility, it would make sense that they would incur a significant number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now, if an attack was conducted by a demilitarised zone, for instance, in your country, against a civilian population, would that demilitarised area lose its status as a demilitarised area or would such attacks be tolerated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not, again, an expert in International Law, but it is my understanding that if one side or one opposing force militarises a particular protected or civilian area, that, depending on the circumstances, it would lose various protections under International Law. Whether a UN-declared demilitarised area has or does not have weight as protected under International Law is a question best left for a different type of expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Can you now just tell us: How is it possible that something could both have and not have the status of a demilitarised area at the same time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to throw out a hypothetical situation: A hospital, by virtue of it being a medical facility, would be protected and consequently is supposed to be demilitarised. If a situation arose that the adversarial military forces occupied that facility for a military reason, perhaps because where the hospital is located and it gave them a tactical military advantage, it would lose its protected status and become a legitimate military target because it was now being used for military purposes and not humanitarian purposes. Having said that, once the military that are occupying that particular facility leave and it again resumes a humanitarian and medical purpose, it resumes its status as a protected facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now, do you know that we've heard the commander of the units that were attacked in the area of the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka testified here, and that from that day of the attack all the way up to the 28th of August he was engaged in carrying out the operations towards --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: ... Han, in Zepa, and he remained there throughout the operations, and was it a justified action by this commander to return his forces to the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's more than one commander at the Crna Rijeka. If the general could help us with -- I think I know who he's talking about, but it would help Mr. Butler to know who, in particular, he's talking about in this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would assist the Chamber as well. Whom are you referring to, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I'm referring to General Savcic, who testified here, and his units were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what I would like to ask Mr. Butler is: Have you read his testimony and the documents and the transcript during your preparation for your expertise here? Did you read all of this? And I'm referring to Mr. Savcic's testimony and transcript and so on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that I read General Savcic's testimony related to this specific set of proceedings. I am generally familiar with General Savcic, who's testified in a number of previous proceedings, and I'm familiar with it there. So it will probably be hit or miss with respect to any new material that General Savcic might have discussed that I'm not aware of. And if you can repeat the second half of your question because it is just -- it's just running off the screen and I wasn't sure that I understood what you were looking for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will rephrase my question to make it clearer. Do you know that General Savcic testified between -- or, rather, from the 26th of June up until the 26th of July, he was tasked with repelling the attack from Zepa and Srebrenica, an attack against the Main Staff, and that he was engaged in the Operation Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I am aware from the documents that particularly with respect to operations related to the Zepa enclave, that units of the 65th Protection Regiment did, in fact, play a major role. With respect to Srebrenica, as I've testified before, at least one of his units, the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment, you know, also played a role in at least the issues relating to not the actual attack on Srebrenica, but prisoners. So in the context of the date range that you have given me, while I don't have specific visibility from the 26th of June to the 10th of July when orders are being issued specific to Zepa, I would certainly not disagree with you by saying that the 65th would have still been involved in at least defensive operations around Veliki Zep and other facilities that they were charged to protect during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. The time has come for our first break. I suggest that you should read Mr. Savcic's testimony and the transcript of that testimony, and after that I will invite you to tell me whether his engagement was justified when he put up resistance against the attack of the forces that had attacked him from the demilitarised zone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would have no objection for Mr. Butler to be able to review General Savcic's testimony at the break. But I think Mr. Butler must need a break, like the rest of us, after all this testimony, and to be doing that kind of work on the break I don't think is realistic. But the large break, I think that would be another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was worrying all the time, especially the task you have to carry out during night-time to read through the document we have dealt with just in the last couple of minutes. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe there has been a misunderstanding. Mr. Tolimir has just recommended to Mr. Butler to read something, not to read it at the break, certainly not. He just recommended Mr. Butler that he should perhaps read it over the summer break, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. We must have our break now, and we'll come back at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just briefly: On page 14, line 20, instead of "trig point 676," it should be "675."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, is this an appropriate time to deal with the translation issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are all P numbers: The first, 847C, then 199, then P770, P1569B, P1678, P1960, P2076A, P2116, P2231, P2351, P2361, P2442, P2443 and, finally, P2448.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These are now received in evidence. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on with your cross-examination and try to focus on matters related to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We can now see the document D62 still in front of us on the screen. I would like to go to the second page. Can this be displayed. Thank you. We're still waiting for the second page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We now see the second page and the second paragraph, where Mr. Palic, the commander of the Zepa Brigade, says: "Our losses are as follows: Two killed, one seriously wounded, and five lightly wounded." Does this show that this report is, indeed, authentic and credible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't question the authenticity of the report or the credibility of the information that Avdo Palic is passing up his particular chain of command to his superiors. My only issue was that I hold open the possibility that the reports that Commander Palic was receiving from his soldiers as to how many killed or wounded they thought they inflicted on the enemy may be higher than had actually occurred and are certainly higher in numbers than I'm used to seeing for a combat action of this type of nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Please look at the third paragraph on the same page, which says, and I quote: "In view of the state of affairs in this brigade's zone of responsibility, we shall do our best to follow consistently the order of the commander of the 2nd Corps, Strictly Confidential 02/1-604/95, which is appropriate and realistic in our circumstances, as well as consistent with the agreement reached at the command post in the Main Staff ..." My question is this: Does this part of Avdo Palic's report show that they had received an order on carrying out combat operations, and that they had visited the command post of the Main Staff of the BiH, where they had received their tasks verbally, which is confirmed by the combat document that they then issued on the said date?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your assertion that the military operations that occurred and future military operations envisioned are doing so on the basis of Strictly Confidential Order 02/1-604/95. I'm not sure that I agree with your assertion that members of the brigade at Zepa personally met with individuals or had personally visited the command post of the Supreme Command of the BiH Army. I suspect that there may be a translation issue in your question that just is being mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could you please look at the English version and look at the fourth paragraph that we see in Serbian. In English, it's the penultimate paragraph, and can you look at the fourth line from the bottom, where it says this is consistent with the agreement reached at the command post in the Main Staff. Does this sentence in the report show, does it prove, that somebody, indeed, presented themselves at the command post of the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree with that. It is my contention that the person who would have presented himself or group that would have presented themselves at the Main Staff are more likely to have come from the Command of the 2nd Corps, speaking on behalf of the officers and commander in Zepa, as opposed to those particular officers in Zepa travelling to the Command of the ABiH Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you read Ramiz Becirovic's statement? And he was the command of the 28th Division, he was a deputy chief of staff during the breakthrough. Did you read it? And did you see that certain officers from the 28th Division did, indeed, present themselves at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I am aware, not only from Mr. Becirovic, but from a number of other documents and sources, that sometime in May or June, maybe even as early as April, the commander of the 28th Division, Naser Oric, as well as a number of his officers, left Srebrenica and the 28th Division and were moved to Tuzla and were outside the enclave. So, again, I take your point that it is entirely possible that members of the 28th Division did personally represent Avdo Palic. My position is that -- and what I'm trying to, apparently not so clearly, state is that I don't think it's likely that Avdo Palic or members of his brigade staff personally attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's your opinion. However, in this report that he sent to his subordinates, who knew whether they had been there or not, why does he say, and I quote: "... as well as consistent with the agreement reached at the command post of the Main Staff"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take that that Colonel Palic is obviously aware of the meetings that took place and that -- the decisions that were reached. It would be natural, even if he was not personally present, that those discussions and the decisions reached would be transmitted to him, as they would impact his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I don't think that this report was sent to the subordinates of Avdo Palic, but to his superiors, if I'm not mistaken. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I may have misspoken. Avdo Palic wrote this to his superiors, and he says "consistent with the agreement at the command post," which means that both him and his addressees are aware of the fact that the operation had been discussed and agreed at the command post where the details of the operation had also been agreed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps we could also look at D52 to show that activities were being carried out in keeping with the November 1994 plan that the Main Staff sent to the 28th Division. Once again, could we please see D52. Yes, we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, this is also a document issued by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by the 2nd Corps Command. It was sent from Tuzla on the 8th of July, 1995. It was sent under the title "Information on Combat Results of the Units and Commands of the 28th Ground Army Division of the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army." Was this report, indeed, sent by the 2nd Corps to its units, and was it sent in order to inform them about the successes of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at the two bullet points under this first paragraph. The first bullet point reads: "Sixty Chetniks were liquidated, and according to unconfirmed reports, the aggressor suffered even greater losses and had many wounded: "Sixteen automatic rifles, three M-72 light machine-guns, one M-53 light machine-gun, one carbine, two radio stations, three pistols, 5.000 bullets, and dozens of head of cattle and small livestock were seized, and one van was destroyed." My question: Did the corps command at that point have access to all information, and did it convey that information to all the other members of the military to tell them what successes had been achieved by the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your first question, I mean, certainly the 2nd Corps had access to the information it was receiving from the 28th Division reporting on the successes of its various activities. I take from the title of this particular document and the fact that it's to -- or from the deputy commander for morale - it's very difficult to tell on the translation - that one of the purposes of this particular document was precisely so that various morale officers could relay this information, after removing any secret material from it, to the broader soldiers and officers of the 2nd Corps in effort to inspire them to seek to emulate the same type of military accomplishments that the soldiers of the 28th Infantry Division were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up to show the signature block and also to whom the document was sent. Can the document be scrolled up a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see that the document was sent to -- we don't see it now. We can see it in Serbian; that it was sent to all divisions - now we have it in English as well - to the commanders of all divisions, to all logistics units, to garrison commanders, to an air force brigade, and this was signed personally by the commander of the 2nd Corps, Brigadier Sead Delic. You can now see who he sent the document to. That was sent by electronic mail, so we cannot see the signature, but his name is typed up. Please, based on everything that you have seen, meaning that the commander refers to written and verbal orders and that operations are carried out from Zepa and Srebrenica and in other parts of the demilitarised zones, would you say that what General Savcic testified about here is justified, and that was that they engaged in combat in order to defend themselves, to prevent further forays, and to actually return the forces that had forayed from Srebrenica and Zepa back to the demilitarised zones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, setting aside for the moment General Savcic's testimony here, what I would say is what I believe I've been very consistent about in the numerous times I've testified before this Tribunal in other cases, as well as in this one, which is that the 28th Infantry Division was never demobilised or demilitarised. It did conduct active military operations through the period of the end of June 1995. And that from my point of view and my opinion, that VRS military operations directed against the 28th Infantry Division were a justified military act. I think I've been relatively consistent with that position through the years. So, again, while I don't know what General Savcic did or did not specifically say, I certainly wouldn't dispute an assertion that he believed that, you know, the military operations that he was conducting against soldiers from the 28th Infantry Division would be legitimate. I mean, I agree that they would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, after having received this answer, I think, again, we see that there is no dispute about the conduct and the acts of the ABiH in relation to this conflict. I would like to invite you more to focus on the charges against you in the indictment and not so much about combat activities. This is not in contest, I take it. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since the beginning of the day I have been looking at documents which prove the attempts by Muslims and their Supreme Command to link up Srebrenica and Zepa with the 2nd Corps in Tuzla and to link up the two enclaves with each other, and I've also looked at documents which have already been received by the Trial Chamber and which demonstrate that that was, indeed, the case. And I'm now trying to proffer proof to show why all the directives were issued, why all the tasks have been given and assigned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just would like to remind you that this trial is not about a war. This trial is about certain criminal acts you are charged with. This is the background of my intervention and my guidance I tried to give you in order to make sure that you will use your time for cross-examination in the best way for your defence. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll do my best. However, I have to answer all the questions or all the issues that were raised by the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief of this witness. Please, let us go back to the order issued on the 11th, bearing number D300, and that was sent by Enver Hadzihasanovic on the 9th of November, 1994. I misspoke. Aleksandar has just corrected me. Let's go back to P2369, and D300 is Directive 6. Thank you very much. I apologise to the e-court. This is a document which was sent by General Enver Hadzihasanovic on the 9th of November, 1994. We were on paragraph 3.3, page 9. We had covered paragraph 2 in Chapter 3.3, and that dealt with sabotage operations that were being carried out in keeping with the order. And now can we go on to look at the same page again, page 10 in this document. Thank you. We can now see that below the title "Zepa forces" it says "The forces of the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army." We have to go to the following page in English, and there we can see tasks being issued under A to OG-6 Zivinice forces. There is a reference to attacks from the territory of the BiH Army towards the demilitarised zones of Zepa and Srebrenica, as well as of activities aimed at linking up the two enclaves and their linking with the 2nd Corps. Now let's look at page 11 -- or, rather, page 10, page 10, where it says they are carrying out an attack, the beginning of page 10, where it says Zivinice forces are carrying out attacks, and "insert armed forces in the following zone." I skip the names of the places. And they are tasked of acting in concert with inserted forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: In this paragraph, the units of the 2nd Corps which bordered on the Republika Srpska, were they given a task to act in concert with the forces of the 28th Division during the breakthrough and during the operation that had been planned previously for the 28th Division? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document, which is dated November 1994, it lists out specific tasks for OG-6 and OG-4 which, as General Tolimir notes, would be along the border -- or along the confrontation lines between ABiH 2 Corps and the VRS. It was envisioned in this plan that all of the military operations would be synchronised and co-ordinated with each other in order to have the maximum adverse impact on the VRS when this operation was undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now please take a look at some three lines or four lines below the "OG-4 Kalesija forces." We have before us the Zivinice forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that should be on page 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, we see those four lines above "OG Kalesija." We see that it says their task, and that's the task of the OG-6, and it reads as follow -- and OG-6, that's the operations group in Zivinice. The task is as follows: "On the axis of attack, disperse and destroy the Chetnik forces and secure the corridor along the right-hand side border of the zone of attack. Link up the forces of OG-6 Srebrenica at this specified line and prevent Chetnik intervention from the direction of Sekovici towards Seliste village and the Borogovo feature (trig point 923)." Now my question: Are these forces that had contact on the territory that had -- these forces that had come from the territory on the 2nd Corps of the BH Army, was it their task to link up with the 28th Division forces, as indicated here under "OG-8 Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If and when this plan was implemented or to be implemented, their task was to link up with those forces of OG-8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was this the basic conceptual plan for the entire operation to link up the enclaves and to link up the forces within the enclaves with the 2nd Corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If we read this document in its entirety, I believe you are correct that it does lay out the basic conceptual plan to achieve that link-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the next page, please. We can leave Kalesija aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you take a look at 4.3, that paragraph. That's under the "General Notes and Tasks," which is Chapter 4. Thank you. "The plan of operation," and I quote, "for time and place of the execution of tasks will be worked out separately and delivered to you subsequently." And my question: Does this suggest that this operation was, indeed, planned, and that the planning was in its final phases of its implementation, and this is something that the units would be informed of? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your assertion that it was planned, in the sense that the basic concept existed. When you read this document, it goes into probably even more detail than a basic concept. But, clearly, my reading of paragraph 4.3 is that there are still other issues, particularly when you read this in context with other statements in the document, that have yet to be worked out, either planned or implemented, that have to be achieved before this entire operation can move forward. And, again, the last line being that, We're identifying those various components that have to be done before we can move forward and we will be alerting you to what our orders and decisions are in a future time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for your answer. You are perhaps referring to paragraph 4.5, which reads, and I quote: "An important and basic precondition to carry out this operation is your supply with the minimum quantity of ammunition and UBS," or combat supplies. Did you mean that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes, sir. As you would obviously know, sending forces out from the OG-8 and, later, 28th Infantry Division without adequate amounts of ammunition and other material -- military materials in order to accomplish these tasks would certainly result in a significant defeat for those forces. So one of the preconditions before this could be executed was that ammunition and other military materials would have to be infiltrated into the enclave and stockpiled in sufficient quantities to allow for these types of operations to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now let's take a look at 4.7, which is where what you've just mentioned is specified, and I quote: "Apart from the task of bringing in the ammunition and war materiel, immediately embark upon the organisation of reconnaissance in the depth of the enemy and the features which are to be seized, and the insertion of men who will later participate in the tasks. Report on the results of the work regularly and promptly." Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in part. I mean, obviously the task of bringing in ammunition. But specific to paragraph 4.7, it notes that another precondition, as it were, is that the OG-8 will need to send out small reconnaissance teams to essentially observe and scout the terrain objectives that they plan to seize at a later date. Knowing, first of all, how to get to that terrain and what all the geographic and terrain issues that have to be dealt with, as well as what VRS military dispositions would be or might be around those particular objectives, would be a vital element of information that would have to be known by OG-8 if they were going to have any chance of success in this military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you agree with me if I say that the main issue here is obtaining ammunition and lethal assets, and everything else is a question of training and equipment -- or, rather, provisions of the army and the units that are to be used for insertions and raids? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I read this -- these points, and I think it goes all the way to point 14, in their entirety, there are three or four basic themes that are laid out here as significant concerns to the General Staff, or the Supreme Command in this case, of the ABiH. One, obviously, is whether or not they would be able to supply the requisite military technical equipment, ammunition, and other military supplies in order to undertake the operation, which, again, given the context of OG-8 being located many kilometres behind enemy lines, was no easy feat. The second one was ensuring that there was available military manpower and soldiers to accomplish the task that had been directed. And so, again, I take General Tolimir's point. It's not just men with guns; there is an implied training requirement. The third issue is, you know, a thorough reconnaissance of the battle-field to include the objectives so that the OG-8 military forces would know where they're going and what they should expect when they get to their objectives. And the last one is the issue of security, which hasn't been discussed yet, but it is a key theme throughout this operations order because it was recognised that with a plan of this complexity, if the VRS were to learn of this plan, particularly at the early stages of the plan, that they could relatively quickly either preclude or prevent the plan from occurring by attacking the forces in the enclave, which would, in effect, cause much of the plan to collapse. So they were very concerned about not only accomplishing all of these things ready to undertake the plan, but to do so in a way that would minimise the risk of the enemy discovering what was being planned and later to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now, in the course of your research, did you come across documents that speak to or about the main command trying to provide the right conditions in order to enable this operation of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not look specifically at ABiH military documents related to the attempts to logistically supply the 28th Infantry Division. However, again referring to the United Nations report related to the fall of Srebrenica, there is some discussion in that particular report where it talks about the UN's awareness of efforts by the ABiH and, specifically, 2 Corps to smuggle military supplies and ammunition into the enclaves during the period the first six months of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D67 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'd like to show you this document, and then I have some questions. We see here that this is a report from the Intelligence Administration, Sarajevo, Counter-Electronic Warfare Department, Communications and Electronic Counter-Measures Section, dated the 13th of July, 1995, in which the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- rather, its Army General Staff, forwards, via the commander of the 1st Corps, to the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina this interim report after the fall of Srebrenica, in which they report on what they had done so far for the enclave, and it reads as follows: "Dear Mr. President. "In view of the situation of our enclaves during the preceding period, the Army General Staff has undertaken a series of military activities and procedures to organise the members of the army in the enclaves and prepare them for possible developments, primarily the defence of the existing free territory and a planned engagement and preparations for future joint operations and planned operations." My question would be this: Do we see here that the commander of the army is pointing out to the president of the state that he's planning planned operations for the defence of the enclaves and with the members of the army in the enclaves? Now we'll see later on who this document was signed by. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just show the signature page, please, by e-court. And then go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If the general is, which it appears he is, planning on asking Mr. Butler detailed questions about this, I am told it's a four-page document, and I think it would only be fair to let Mr. Butler review this document before questions are posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it depends on the question Mr. Tolimir is putting to the witness. We will see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Butler, as well as the Trial Chamber. We saw the signature page. We saw who it was who signed this document. Can we now have the first page again, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And, witness, sir, could you please tell us whether we see from this document that Delic had informed Izetbegovic that he was preparing the enclaves for future joint operations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. I mean, I have seen this document before. It turns out in my previous testimony in the Perisic case there was a rather spirited discussion about helicopter flights into the Srebrenica enclave, so I am familiar with this particular document. Again, in this context, as issues are coming up on the 13th of July, 1995, and questions are being raised, this is a report to the highest levels of the BiH government, where the military justifies, to some degree, the support that they have given to the enclave, and lays out in some specific detail all of the activities that they undertook in order to get supplies into the enclave. Clearly, in the context that General Tolimir has raised, the language does imply that this was not just routine supplies, so to speak; that there was at least some -- you know, there was not only, I guess, you know, the primary defence of the existing free territory, so I guess in some sense it is routine resupply, but also discusses preparations for future operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And now would you take a look, please, below the first paragraph. It says: "Specifically, the following has been done for Srebrenica and Zepa:" And then bullet point 1: "To start with, lethal assets and MTS/materiel and technical equipment were brought in on foot in fairly small quantities." And then the second bullet point: "Seventeen helicopter flights were carried out, in each of which a helicopter was hit." And now can we see the page following a number of bullet points there and see the last bullet point where the table begins. It says: "The attached table shows exactly what MTS was delivered to Srebrenica and Zepa." And then it gives a breakdown of that materiel in a table. Now, the question is this: Did the Main Staff of the BH ensure, via these helicopter flights, that the enclaves in Srebrenica and Zepa received sufficient equipment and supplies in order to carry out attacks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, either -- I mean, ultimately, just like in the context of the VRS, it was the Main Staff that was undertaking those activities through corps and other subordinate formations. In this manner, the ABiH Supreme Command undertook, either directly or through 2nd Corps, operations to try and get ammunitions and other military technical supplies to Srebrenica and Zepa. The fact that military operations were carried out to the degree that they were, you know, would reflect that, at least in hindsight, they were getting enough ammunition and enough supplies to conduct the operations that they did conduct. The unknown question is whether or not they ever received an adequate amount of materiel and supplies to reach the threshold to conduct the large-scale operation that was envisioned down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now please take a look at this table, and will you see, under number 1, it says Zepa receives 173.600 rounds, where Srebrenica receives 354.658; in total, 469.228 [as interpreted] rounds. And then in the following rows we see 7.62-millimetre rounds - that's number 2 - three 7.9 millimetres, 9.400 pieces. 4, we see that 7.9 rounds are mentioned -- or, rather, that's number 3.
