Number 4 is "rifle-launched grenade." Cumulative contact-fuse grenades. And then five contact-fuse rifle-launch grenades, and six hand-grenade, seven RPG, et cetera, et cetera. You know what RPGs is. Perhaps you can explain it to the Trial Chamber, where it says "390." So what is RPG-7 rocket?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As noted under asset seven, it's translated as "rocket-propelled grenade." RPG-7 is the traditional Soviet military model, which is ubiquitously copied by everyone of a hand-held rocket-grenade launcher. It fires the RPG-7 rockets. So what this reflects is a number of rocket-launchers as well as extra rockets for them. It's a hand-held device. It's, again, pretty common within most light military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could you please tell us whether you know from the documents when the ammunition and weapons were air-dropped. Do you know when Muslims started doing that in 1995 and for how long that whole operation lasted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge of that is based off of the information in the United Nations report. And if I recall correctly, I think those types of resupply operations began sometime in the early part of 1995. I don't think I could be much more specific than that. It's been a number of years since I've dealt with that particular issue. I would again refer -- if it is an issue -- a question that, in fact, needs to be dealt with, I would refer the Court to that particular United Nations report, where it is laid out in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Thank you for referring us to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we have in e-court, on the right-hand side where the Serbian -- where the Serbian document is now, can we see 65 ter 420 in English. I have the Serbian hard copy, so I can read from it. And now we can see the document. I would kindly ask for the table to remain on the left-hand side. This is a document issued by the 28th Division, the Command of the OG-8 Srebrenica, dated 15 November 1994. The title of the document is "The Main Plan for the Execution of Task/Opinion," sent to the Staff of the Supreme Command and Enver Hadzihasanovic in Kakanj. Can we go to the last page to see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be instructed to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, two issues. E-court didn't understand your instruction correctly. You wanted to have D67 in English on the left-hand side of the screen, and especially the table; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Mr. President. If that is possible, fine. If not, we'll go back to it later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to understand what your instructions are. You wanted to have on the left-hand side D67 in English; is that correct? And what did you want to have on the right-hand side? Is that the document we have now on the screen, also in English, if I understood you correctly, because you have the English -- the B/C/S version in front of you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But on the right-hand side we have a Serbian version, whereas I would like to have the English version of the document, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And this is 65 ter 420 in English, please, if that is possible. You wanted to have on the left-hand side D67. Now we have it on the right-hand side, D67. And on the other side of the screen we wanted to do have 65 ter 402, both in English. I think we have it now. Again, now this is identical. There we are. I think we have it now on the screen. Mr. Tolimir, please carry -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have not finished. Just a moment. The interpreters asked you to slow down while reading. Now continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the document on the right-hand side, which is in English, be brought back to page 1. We need to read just one sentence from that page. Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading the first sentence: "I have received and carefully studied your basic plan to execute the task. I wish to set out my views and suggestions in this respect. "Item 1 - plan acceptable. "Item 2 - acceptable. "Item 3 - engagement of forces ..." And so on and so forth. And now he says, and I will not go on reading, he provides his opinion about the deployment of combat groups. And finally at the end of the document where you can see the signature we would like to look at the last paragraph on the last page in Chapter 12, under the title "General Remarks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Look at the screen, at the transcript. You see you are reading too fast. The interpreters can't follow. You want to have everything on the screen -- on the transcript, and, therefore, you should slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the Trial Chamber and to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's now look at what Mr. Oric says about what he needs for the execution of the task. The following quantities of ammunition have to be brought in to carry out the task. In the left-hand-side table, we can see that he received 354.000 rounds, and he requested only 173.000, so he's received three times more. He also asks for 55.000 other types of rounds, and we see that he has 7.62, 24.000, and Zepa has 4.360. And then further on he says that he needs 150 hand-held or rifle-launched grenades, and he also has contact-fuse rifle-launched grenades, and so on and so forth. My question is this: Was Mr. Oric supplied by air with all the necessary ammunition and weapons that he had requested for the operation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I can answer that, because the one outstanding bit of information that's needed would be the answer of, well, you know, consumption. In abstract, 469.000 rounds of ammunition delivered sounds like a lot and would be sufficient to stockpile for an operation of this nature. One has to take in account that these supplies are being consumed in other military operations or in defence of the enclave from VRS attacks. So from these two documents, you know, the one part of the equation that's missing in order to determine whether or not he was able to successfully stockpile what he needed for the operation is a view of what the 28th Division was consuming as part of their normal military requirements. So, I mean, if they're consuming 600.000 rounds during the same period and have only been resupplied to a 469.000-rounds level, then the answer is, no, he wasn't receiving the necessary supplies. If they only used 100.000 rounds, then the answer might be, yes, he received three times as many -- or three times as much ammunition as he thought he needed. But without facts and figures relating to the consumption of the military units, at the same time it can be misleading to answer the question whether or not resupply was adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Please, before the operation started, was the demilitarised zone supposed to carry out any operations? Were they supposed to use ammunition once it was demilitarised? Could we then, in that case, talk about whether any ammunition was spent or not spent? What I mean is -- mean to say is that it should have been demilitarised and weapons should have been seized from them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in abstract, I agree. If -- if the zone was demilitarised as envisioned, your ammunition consumption numbers would be zero. We know, though, that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You're a military analyst and a researcher. Could you tell us whether the commander who has received a task should stockpile for an operation, in view of the fact that he received his stocks by air, under the control of the UNPROFOR, who were in a position to control every helicopter sound in the air? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, getting to your first question, a commander who envisions on conducting military operations will obviously take the prudent and necessary steps to stockpile not only ammunition, but what other military supplies he believes he will need in order to conduct that operation. Of course, he has to do so in context of the other military requirements that he has at the time. So what he knows he needs to do and what may be practicable under the circumstances could be different. I don't know that I can answer the second question with respect to the UNPROFOR having control of the air and things of that nature. I mean, that's a -- I don't know that that has to be answered. It's simply, yes, they did resupply not only over land, but by helicopter resupply flights that have been documented, so, I mean, the answer is, yes, they were getting resupplied. And, yes, a prudent commander would stockpile his supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D53 is the following document I would like to call up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have used 65 ter 420. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Thank you, Mr. President, for reminding me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 420 shall be assigned Exhibit D302. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at D53. Thank you. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see an order here? This order was issued by the BiH Army on the 17th of June, and there is a reference to active combat operations. And I'm going to read just the first paragraph: "Pursuant to a verbal order issued --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could the -- yes, thank you. I was asking for enlargement of the B/C/S version. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Pursuant to a verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BiH Army, Army General Rasim Delic, and on the occasion of the great successes achieved by units of the BiH Army in the general area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence that the command of the aggressor forces of the Protection Regiment in Han Pijesak is holding part of its units in reserve to intervene in the event of an attack by our forces from Zepa, I hereby issue the following order: "Execute all preparations in the Command of the 28th Land/Army Division to execute offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of BiH Army, over-extending the aggressor forces and inflicting losses on them, co-ordinating action with the BiH Army forces carrying out operations in the general area of Sarajevo." And the second bullet point reads: "Plan realistic tasks which will assure certain success, on the basis of an accurate assessment and the potential of our forces in Srebrenica and Zepa." My question to you is this: The person who drafted this document, who was issuing the order, as well as the person who received the order, should both have the realistic view or should they have both made a realistic assessment of their military capabilities for the execution of this task? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I read your question correctly, sir, what you're asking is that as an order is passed down from the higher levels through intermediate levels to the command that's required to execute it, is there a process by which the various commands evaluate orders that are received and make determinations as to whether or not they can fully carry them out, or partially carry them out, or carry them out only to a limited degree. I mean, that is a normal command function. Is that the question that you're asking, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what I asked you: The person who issued the order to execute the task and the person who was supposed to execute it, did they both have to have in mind realistic assessments of the consumption of materiel, lethal assets, and other resources necessary for the execution of the task? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In that sense, both the intervening individual -- or intermediate individual, in this case General Budakovic, as well as the individuals who received this order would be expected to tailor the tasks to what is realistically possible. So in order to do that, they would know whether or not they had all of the necessary equipment, supplies, materiel, and manpower to accomplish that task. It doesn't make any military sense to plan to execute a task that you know that you can't accomplish because you're lacking in other components of military ammunition or supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you notice, in the first paragraph of this order, that a reference is made to offensive operations, with a view to liberating the territory? And when we're talking about these assessments, did they also take into account the task to liberate the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? In other words, was there an opinion that the commander -- commanders of the BiH Army were capable of ultimately doing that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this particular order is far more limited than I would take your question to mean. This order is simply, and quite cleverly, actually, a reflection of the fact that the Bosnian and Herzegovina military has learned that the 65th Protection Regiment has still managed to maintain a considerable amount of reserve forces which could, conceivably, be employed in the Sarajevo area, and, in fact, the 65th Protection Regiment was, throughout the course of the war, deployed in many various areas of the Republika Srpska because it represented a mobile and powerful reserve force. And so based on this information, this reads to me like the 2nd Corps and their 28th -- and the 28th Infantry Division are being directed to put together a military attack out of Srebrenica or Zepa, the primary purpose to ensure that the 65th Protection Regiment is held in place there or is engaged in that particular location and that their reserves are then exhausted or over-extended. And, therefore, it would not be available to be redeployed to the Sarajevo and Gorazde battle-front area which, in the words of the BiH Army at this juncture, was the critical battle that was going on. I don't take this particular document to read in such a wide-sweeping manner as you suggested that, you know, this is their expectation, that they're going to be able to liberate all of the territory of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read paragraph 1 once again, where it says, and I read again: "Execute all preparations in the Command of the 28th Land/Army Division to execute offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." This was signed by Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic. Does it mean that he has in mind the liberation of the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and all those tasks that have to be executed during offensive operations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I take this simply as view of liberating the territory of BH to the extent that they are already doing in the wider area around Sarajevo and Gorazde. Obviously a war aim of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was going to be to liberate all of their territory of all the territory that they considered occupied, but I just -- in this particular singular document, I just don't read as much into it as you do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's time for the second break. We have to adjourn, and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I asked you whether the chief of staff of the 2nd Corps, Brigade General Budakovic, was referring to an oral order and ordered the preparations, that they be made for combat operations. So was he actually relying on Delic's order when he issued his order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears, in part, as you look at the preamble on that first paragraph, it says, one: "Pursuant to a verbal order ..." and, of course, it also refers back to an earlier document. But looking at this in its entirety, I would say that, again, this order was written in the context of receiving a verbal order from Delic, who wanted various supporting actions done to ensure that the ABiH military forces around Sarajevo and Gorazde could continue to enjoy success.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And could that be the oral order that was issued to the chiefs of staffs of command that was issued to -- in the Command of the 28th Land/Army Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. Are you asking that this particular document, and as it was set out by General Budakovic, was this document based, in large degree, to the oral order?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was whether Budakovic was talking about the oral order from Delic that should be known not only to him, but also to those who sent the document; in other words, members of the Command of the 28th Division. And how could he refer to the order if they were not -- if they didn't have information on what it contained?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I agree with your assertion that this is the order that Budakovic sent to the Command of the 28th Division. It was, to a large degree, it appears, based on a verbal order. And I also agree that given the document reference in question, that it does presuppose that the Command of the 28th Division in Srebrenica has a working knowledge of that particular document as well as the general situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's see whether the Command of the 28th Division could have been informed of the oral order of the commander. Could we now see document D1, 1D1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should switch off your microphone during your private discussion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see here a statement from the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division where he speaks about his being at the command post in Kakanj with the Chief of Staff and the commander, because that was their command post, the BH Army command post, in April 1995. And maybe that is when he received the oral order, because there was no other way he could receive it. Now, let's take a look at page 5 in Serbian and 7 in English. Now we see in Serbian, in paragraph 4, which reads, and that's the second paragraph in English --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is not the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Towards the end of April, we flew out of Zepa in a helicopter" -- My error. I was asking for the English page. So: "In late April 1995, we flew by helicopter from Zepa and arrived in Zenica. We were part of a delegation sent from Srebrenica, headed by Commander Naser Oric ..." And so on and so forth. He goes on to name all the others who were there. They had a task, and so on and so forth. Now, does this suggest that it was possible for him to have had a contact, oral contact, with the Chief of Staff, including the order to begin combat operations and try a break-out from Srebrenica towards the 2nd Corps in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess where I'm -- I'm having difficulty following the track on this is the document that we just discussed, you know, how that relates to this particular date and time. I mean, can we go back to that original document? I mean, I just want to, in my own mind, go back to the date of the document that you were referencing earlier and then try and compare it to this particular oral order, or a written order, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall the document that was published on the 11th of November, 1994, relating to the break-out operation and the linking up of enclaves? Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see that this document speaks of April 1995, in other words, a period following that period from that document? And now if you look at the seventh line below the line containing the words "April 1995," where it says: "Commander Oric and I were supposed to go back together, but after a discussion with the commander of the General Staff, Oric received permission to stay on in Tuzla for a while and to return to Srebrenica after the training of officers, around the 10th of May, of officers who had come for training earlier." Now, can we see from this that there was oral communication between the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division with the commander of the General Staff, and that they were there from April 1995 until the 10th of May, 1995, when Naser Oric stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see if I can cut right to what I believe you are driving to. If I understood the text of the various questions correctly, are you asking me that do I believe that in this period of April/May 1995 the activities that you are discussing here are, in fact, the verbal order to implement this particular plan that we've discussed, 02-1/1394-1, dated 9 November 1994? Is that the question that you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question to you is in line with what you've just said. Now, was Commander Delic, the commander of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, did he have oral communication with the commander and Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, as stated here by Ramiz Becirovic in his statement, in other words, from late April into May? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have communicated with him in a variety of ways. As you know, the -- not only could they have done oral communications, but there was the ability to do written communications or enciphered computer communications, so I would not limit contacts just to oral communications. Clearly, if the individual was out of the enclave, that did increase or would increase the ability to communicate in person, let alone orally over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I pointed out a meeting that they had where they had direct contact, and this is something that Becirovic talked about. And then I said that it was not possible to have any further contact unless there was communication or visits. Here, he described a visit, and then it also says: "... pursuant to an oral order from the BiH commander, carry out preparations for combat operations in order to liberate the territory of the BH Army." That's how this letter or order began. Now, my question to you is: Could Delic issue this oral order, about when the operation was to begin and the plan implemented, could he have done that earlier because they were there for training and preparations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- just to qualify one point. As I noted, I do not read that order in the same way that you did, that it qualifies as a full-blown liberation-of-the-territory order. Having said that, having -- General Delic could have clearly issued the order, either orally or in writing, at any time that he deemed that the conditions were met to begin the final preparations for the plan that we've talked about for 9 November 1994. Having all of the relevant commanders physically present, or many of them present in Tuzla, would have had an opportunity to do that, if, in fact, he chose to do it there. As a military practice, having the subordinate commanders and key principals around and physically being able to brief them on the order helps to ensure that everyone understands what the tasks are and what is expected of them. So, you know, while the order may have been given at that point in time, if I agreed to your time-line and assertion, the actual final preparations for the operation would clearly not have started occurring until such time that all of those relevant individuals who were in Tuzla were brought back into the enclave so they could undertake the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now please answer this question: Was the direct, personal, physical, as it were, contact between Naser Oric, his deputy, Ramiz Becirovic, and the commander of the BH Army, Rasim Delic [Realtime transcript read in error "Naser Oric"] in existence, as it were, on this date, on the 5th of this month, where Ramiz Becirovic mentions here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I mean, I can't go into his statement to verify what is or is not or would not have happened. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I note we have a problem in the transcript. In the last question of Mr. Tolimir, there's a reference to "Naser Oric," his "principal." I don't know if he really said "principal" or "deputy," Ramiz Becirovic, and the commander of the BH Army. And we see again the name "Naser Oric." But I think we heard "Rasim Delic." Is that correct, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will clarify all this by quoting the words of Ramiz Becirovic that can be found in his statement in paragraph 3 -- or, rather, the seventh line of that paragraph. That's the paragraph beginning with the words: "In late April 1995." And the seventh line in that paragraph reads: "Commander Oric and I were supposed to go back. But after a discussion with the commander of the General Staff, Oric received permission to stay on in Tuzla for a while and to return to Srebrenica after the training of officers was completed around the 10th of May, officers who had arrived earlier."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, my question is this: Mr. Butler, from this statement of Mr. Becirovic's, can we conclude that there was oral communication between General Delic, Naser Oric, and Ramiz Becirovic in the months of April or May 1995, as described here by Becirovic in his statement, and is it possible that it was at this time that he issued the oral order that was mentioned in document D53 and that I quoted earlier, the document dated 17 June? Thank you. In other words, were they already in the know about the substance of Delic's oral order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean to sound obstinate, but I'm not sure that I can answer that question. This is a statement by a particular individual. I'm not in a position to make conclusions based off of one statement, particularly the conclusions that you're looking for. My answer would be that maybe Mr. Becirovic would be the person that you should be directing that question to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not insist. You conducted an analysis here, and my question now is very specific. Did Ramiz Becirovic state in his statement that he and Naser Oric had direct contact with Rasim Delic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- again, what it says in this statement, it says in the statement. There's -- there's one particular line: "In the meantime, the commander of the General Staff, Delic, arrived, who enable us to go to Visca by helicopter, and we went to a location in the corps command, where Delic received us." Again, I can verify that it says what it says in the statement, but I can't verify that what is said in the statement actually happened, you know, at least in the context of that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We will waste no more time on this. Let the Trial Chamber have their own opinion of this. But let's see now document D178. This is an intelligence information or intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before this will be brought up, please, I would like to see the first and the last page of the current document, which seems to be D1 or 1D1; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now only the B/C/S version on the screen. Thank you. It's a document from the 11th of August, 1995. And I would like to see the last page with the signature. It says signed by Ramiz Becirovic. Thank you very much. Now the other document, D178, should be brought up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: D178 is on the screen now. It says here, in the title, "Main Staff of the VRS, Intelligence and Security Sector." It says "22nd of June, 1995." And, finally, we will see the stamp, on which the date is the 23rd of June or April 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document should be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at the fourth paragraph in this document on page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote -- I apologise, and I quote from the fourth paragraph: "It has been confirmed that the Muslim forces in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde are continuing with preparations for offensive operations, and that they are using the Srebrenica-Zepa axis for the manoeuvre of forces and the movement of civilians and goods. They are supplying ammunition and weapons by air. A great deal of the population is expressing fear and the wish to leave the enclave because of the announced escalation of combat operations and the feeling of isolation." Thank you. End of quote. My question is this: Do you see that on the 22nd of April the Main Staff had information that in Srebrenica preparations were ongoing for an offensive aimed at linking up the enclaves and ultimately linking up the enclaves with the forces of the 2nd Corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says is that the Main Staff had confirmed that the forces in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde are continuing their preparations for offensive operations. It does not say in this particular passage the second assertion that you've made, and -- that it is that these particular offensive operations are designed to link up with the forces of 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at D238.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you're an analyst, a soldier, I have asked you to analyse certain data. That's what my questions have all been for. And now let's first look at page 1. The document was issued on the 26th of June, 1995. It is intelligence information by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the Intelligence and Security Sector. And now can we please look at page 2 in Serbian and 3 in English, where it says in the second paragraph, and I quote: "In the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Muslim Corps, an additional mobilisation campaign is underway, including under-age, elderly, and ill military conscripts. In the area of Majevica, Teocak, Kalesija, and Kladanj, the units of the 2nd Muslim Corps have continued their diversionary operations." And so on and so forth. My question is this -- end of quote. My question is this: Based on this intelligence, can you conclude that when a mobilisation campaign is underway, under-age, elderly, and ill military conscripts are being mobilised as part of that campaign, can you conclude, based on that, that that military is preparing for a serious or large-scale military operation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the sense that offensive operations generally require more from the attacking forces in defend -- than in terms of manpower, equipment, and other issues, if the 2nd Muslim Corps, in this context, is preparing for a significant military operation, it would be logical that they would take whatever steps that they believed they could take in order to ensure that, at least in terms of manpower, they had as many soldiers available as they could in that particular context. Now, having said that, if you're mobilising under-aged, elderly, or ill individuals, particularly with respect to under-age or elderly, I mean, you really are looking in a situation where there will have to be some time spent training or re-training them in order to perform even basic military functions. So it differs, in a sense, from, you know, mobilising relatively well-trained reservists who can be put into combat operations in a week or two, versus drafting a recent group of 16-year-old kids who were formerly in high school and who have had no military service and expecting them to be available in the same time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for this military analysis. And now can you look at the last paragraph on the same page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document in Serbian be scrolled up a little. Thank you. In English, it's 5, page 5, the second paragraph on page 5. Thank you. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to quote from this paragraph: "On 25/26 June of this year, Muslim forces of the 28th Division started offensive operations from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa by infiltrating several sabotage and terrorist groups into our territory. In Srebrenica, they blocked UNPROFOR, accusing them that they had not protected the so-called demilitarised zone. It is not unlikely that parts of UNPROFOR had been disarmed." However, the next sentence reads: "The objective of these operations is to link up our forces and create more favourable conditions for operations by the 24th, 23rd, and 26th Divisions from the directions of Kalesija, Zivinice, and Kladanj." My question to you, sir, is this: Does all this point to the fact that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including its parts in the demilitarised zone, had launched an operation to create a corridor to infiltrate sabotage groups into the territory and that they had started the operation which was planned already in November 1994? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, can I request a clarification on your question. When you read that particular paragraph to me, the English-language translation that I have said: "The objective of these operations is to tie up our forces and create more favourable conditions ..." What I heard you ask -- or you say is: "The objective of these operations is to link up our forces ..." Is it a -- am I -- is the English translation correct, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have an answer to that. But if I could have just a minute or two at the end just to seek a bit of clarification on a 98 bis issue before we leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we should come to an end. We have only three minutes left, and I would like to say some words as well before we break. I think this is going to be a longer discussion and examination of the witness on this document. Is that correct? And, therefore, you should reserve this kind of questions for the next hearing in August. Is that acceptable for you, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Everything is acceptable to me. However, I would really appreciate to receive an answer at least to my last question before we go to the recess. The recess is going to be long, and the witness can be influenced in all sorts of ways, so I would really appreciate an answer before we break up for the summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then you should please say again if -- read this part of the sentence where we see -- which starts with: "The objectives of these operations is to tie up," or "to link up." That was the question. Otherwise, the witness is not able to answer your question. Read this part into the transcript again, please, but only the beginning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am reading that part of the text that you requested. You have it in English: "The objective of these operations is most probably to -- the linking up of our forces and creating more favourable conditions for operations by the 24th, 23rd, and 26th Divisions from the direction of Kalesija, Zivinice and Kladanj." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was only the question of "link up" or "tie up." Now we heard for the first time "it is most probably." Did you say that? I don't see it in the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English translation it should read "most probably the linking up of our forces." Thank you. This is what the English translation should read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you comment on that, Mr. Butler? No, we don't have so much more time. Let's hear the answer of Mr. Butler, if he is able to provide us with the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I were to take it that the actual phrase is translated as "linking up" versus "tying up," the short answer would be: It's possible. I wouldn't necessarily conclude that, because the problem over this whole course of questions and pieces of evidence was that we have one particular document dated 9 November, and in this particular practice I'm being shown disparate pieces of information, to a degree out of context, in a manner to try and to determine whether or not it supports or doesn't support a specific conclusion. As an analyst, that's a particularly bad practice, because you're going to -- you're going to find what you're looking for in this particular case. Now, if you want it to be this way, you can always make a case that it is. You know, it is possible. And if I were to review all of the relevant material, I might even conclude that General Tolimir would be correct. But I would certainly not be comfortable in doing it off of three or four or five pieces of data and jumping to that particular conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. That should conclude now the interrogation of the witness. I give the floor to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have been speaking to Mr. Gajic about the 98 bis, and he is unable to tell me whether or not the general has decided to make a 98 bis argument. I would request the Court require them to tell us before the close of the period until the recess so that we know, in the recess, whether or not we need to be starting to get prepared, because if so, that's when we'll start to get prepared. And I would also like to know: Are you anticipating that this be an argument, if it does happen, by General Tolimir or Mr. Gajic? I've got to go back and read your ruling on that, but I don't -- I'm not sure it will answer the question, but it would be nice to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I clearly can answer your second question. The 98 bis submission should be made by Mr. Tolimir, not by Mr. Gajic. It is not his role in the courtroom to address the Chamber on that. Mr. Tolimir, you have heard the question of Mr. McCloskey. Can you give us an indication if there will be an oral submission pursuant to Rule 98 bis or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I heard your remarks this morning. The Defence has not proffered all its evidence, and we've seen the practice here that even in re-examination new documents were being shown, and the Prosecution has not yet completed its case. Now, after the Prosecution has completed its case, the Defence will decide, and only then, whether or not it will offer its oral submissions within the three hours, as the Trial Chamber informed us. That was in accordance with the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, there is no possibility to put any pressure on the accused today. We will consider this situation, but I would like to invite Mr. Tolimir to consider the situation as well, because it will be not only a burden for the Defence, but also for the Prosecution and the Chamber, to prepare these submissions and decisions. And, therefore, we and the Prosecution would like to know, as soon as possible and as early as possible, about your intentions to make these submissions or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The phrase itself, "oral submissions," suggests that its content does not need to be advised of in advance, because it is oral arguments and they will be made at the time when they are made. So this will be within the three hours, as recommended by the Trial Chamber, and it shouldn't pose any problem either to the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not considered this proposal yet, but there are Trial Chambers in this Tribunal who set a time-line, a time until which you should indicate if you will make such a submission or not. Today we will not issue any such order. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, briefly, one last request that I would make to the general is that if he would please consider providing a targeted 98 bis decision -- or argument to the specific areas that he is concerned with. This has been the practice among Chambers and -- in the past, to direct the Defence to be targeted. Otherwise, it's the Prosecution's burden to respond to everything in the indictment, from the crime base to each element of the crime, which, of course, in three hours is not possible. So that if -- I would request that they make every effort to provide a targeted approach to any submissions. That would be of great help. And I will, of course, discuss this with Mr. Gajic. And if it looks like we're going in that direction, fine. If not, we may request -- we may provide you a filing on that in order to help us be able to direct our three-hour submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the situation and certainly not issue any order today, but we are open for any proposals by the parties and invite the parties to discuss the matter further. But we have to consider the best way to prepare any 98 bis submissions and decisions. This is, I think, an appropriate time to -- although we are running out of time, to thank many people and to express our gratitude for their patience and their support. First of all, the witness, Mr. Butler, you have spent many, many hours and days here in the courtroom, and it will not be the end of this exercise. We thank you very much for your attendance here and for providing us with your experience and the results of your review of documents. Thank you for that. Please be reminded, and I say that with all respect after the comment of Mr. Tolimir, it is not allowed to have contact with the Prosecution or the Defence during the break about the content of your testimony. I think you know that, but I just want to remind you because of the length of the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We, the Chamber, would like to thank others as well, and I would like to mention them. First of all, the Security, please forward that to the other members of the Security who help us, that everything is going very smoothly. I would like to thank the interpreters for their hard work and for their support. Not to forget the technical staff. We have sometimes faced some technical problems, and they helped us without disturbing the proceedings in the courtroom, but especially behind the scene. I would like to thank the Court Officer and all the Court Ushers who have helped us during the last months. And I would like to thank the team of the Defence for preparing the procedure, and the team of the Prosecution, as well as the team of the Chamber. Deliberately I left out one man who is sitting here, and he should write it correctly into the transcript. I would like to thank all the court reporters who had really done a tremendous job to have a correct record of everything that was said, and especially the court reporter who is present today, because it's his last day in this Tribunal, and we wish him all the best for his future and for the next stages of his personal career. Thank you very much to everybody. We adjourn. And we will resume on Monday, the 22nd of August, this year. We adjourn.
